title: 5 days Upper Lower program review (part. 1)
summary: NH reviews week one of a viewer's (OP) 5-day, two-week rotating upper/lower program. He praises the flexible 'gentleman split' and the antagonist supersets but cuts excessive isolation and posterior chain accessories, swaps lat pulldowns for pull-ups, machine deadlifts for barbell ones and box squats for paused squats, and trims days around a few compounds plus supersets.
claims: Removing the rigid limits of upper/lower or PPL while keeping the structure (a 'gentleman split') is more flexible and beneficial
Supersetted exercises don't need matching rep ranges; it's often better not to match, though extreme mismatches have issues
Incline bench 4x7-10 is fine, but lat pulldowns benefit more from 8-12
NH dislikes lat pulldowns; pull-ups are better for hypertrophy, especially weighted
Supersetting a horizontal press with a horizontal pull is smart because the upper back tolerates a lot of volume; antagonist protection is secondary
Seal rows don't involve legs or lower back, so they're one of the few horizontal pulls NH would program with lower reps and higher intensity
Use straps if grip fatigues on high-volume rows
Machines and isolation are important for a physique but must not replace compound movements
Bench is the one lift you can get away with not treating as strict strength work
For a 4-set evolving range, 8-10 is too narrow; use 3x8-10 or 4x8-12
Safety squat bar squats are amazing
Plate-loaded deadlift machines with side handles limit the hip hinge and hamstring stretch; do RDLs with a barbell
Instead of hip thrust machine, GHD, reverse hyper and leg curls, do barbell RDLs 4x8-12 plus one isolation like hip thrusts or reverse hypers
15-20 reps is a good range for calf raises; two calf exercises back to back is fine only if you can progress on both
Twisting oblique work is unnecessary; leg raises and compounds work the obliques plenty
Pick two ab exercises per day and progress on them rather than four
Fewer exercises per muscle allows supersetting different muscles, which saves time and improves progression
SSB squats are more posterior chain than barbell squats, so the program may lack quad work
Pronated T-bar rows hit more upper back and rear delts than neutral grip
Horizontal rows shouldn't be strength work because they require warmed-up legs and lower back
4x6-10 is an excellent rep range for progression
Two presses and two pulls in one day is the upper limit of movement pattern repetitions for most people
Add skull crushers for long head triceps when the program is heavy on presses
Free weights give better biceps results than cable curls
Upper body days naturally look more crowded than lower body days because of the many small muscles that respond to isolation
Too many exercises per day mitigates progression, makes tracking hard and pushes you into irrelevant intensity windows
Leg days are hard but not complicated: two lines on paper, hell to do
Box squats don't recruit more quads, whatever studies say; most people turn them into a hip hinge without stretching the quads
Deadlift machines don't load the spinal erectors and posterior chain like real deadlifts; use a barbell
2x10 on a pull from the floor is too much volume; lower sets give better deadlift hypertrophy results
Choose one posterior chain isolation that decompresses the spine and sacrum and improves hamstring flexibility to prevent tears when deadlifting heavy
If you must squat and deadlift on the same day, squat first, because the squat's negative puts the lumbar spine at risk when fatigued
Replace box squats with paused squats for 7-10 reps, then deadlift one set of five, slowly ramping up
Overhead press is preferred for shoulders; Viking press is fine if you like the neutral grip
NH dislikes the JM press as a hybrid lift that's hard on the elbows; use skull crushers for long head and close-grip bench for lateral/medial heads
High reps on the JM press prevent freak injury but invite overuse injury
More bodyweight vertical pulls should be programmed
15-20 reps on seal rows is too high and enters irrelevant intensity windows
Rear delt fly and side raises at 4x15-20 is too high; 4x12-15 is better
Shrugs are an exception: 15-20 reps is fine
Most people try to do too much; 20-30% of their training does nothing and even hurts them
exercises: no leg/low back involvement; can go heavier
amazing; more posterior chain than back squat
handles at sides limit hip hinge; doesn't replicate deadlift
more upper back and rear delt
becomes a hip hinge; not good for quads
